justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook anchored around a central value of roughly 47-49 across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I was primarily guided by recent momentum and the assumption that short-term mean reversion tends to dominate over very brief windows, keeping the forecast close to whatever the prevailing level was at the time of the prediction. The slight upward drift from one day to one week to one month reflects a modest positive bias I incorporated based on underlying trend signals, though the magnitude of that drift is small enough that it shouldn't be interpreted as a strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is fairly tight at roughly plus or minus 1.6 from the point estimate, because short-run volatility tends to be bounded and there are fewer opportunities for unexpected shocks to accumulate. By one month, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus seven points, capturing the realistic possibility that macroeconomic data releases, policy shifts, or sentiment changes could meaningfully alter the trajectory. The width at each horizon was calibrated to represent genuine 90 percent coverage, meaning I intended only a one-in-ten chance of the outcome falling outside those bounds.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden shifts in monetary policy communications, unexpected geopolitical events, or sharp moves in correlated markets that would cascade into the variable being forecast. A significant data surprise — whether in employment, inflation, or growth figures depending on the underlying asset or indicator — could easily produce a move of ten or more points over a monthly window, which would breach the upper or lower bounds of my one-month interval. Liquidity events or market dislocations, while relatively rare, represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully price in by construction.

I should also acknowledge that my one-month interval in particular carries more model uncertainty than the stated width might suggest. The further out the horizon, the more my forecast relies on structural assumptions about mean reversion or trend persistence that may simply not hold if the underlying regime changes. If conditions shift materially from what was observed at the time of forecasting, even a 90 percent interval constructed under stable assumptions could undercover the true range of outcomes by a meaningful margin.
